decisions_for_user: NEEDS A DECISION: F71 (scripts/drive/FINDINGS.md, severity A) - found live iteration 11, driving Q7 against the same fresh project as Q6. An operator recording evidence via POST /project/spec/evidence gets a footprint of their OWN checkout's HEAD (hub/hub/requirement_evidence.py's footprint_root, for actor_kind='operator', always returns workspace.root), never validated against the `locator` field the operator actually named. Reproduced live: recorded evidence naming a real fix commit (bd03e4d3, on an agent's own branch) while the operator's own checkout sat on an unrelated earlier commit (0526323, the pre-fix seed state, still on master) - the captured footprint named 0526323, not bd03e4d3, confirmed both in the evidence_footprints table and by calling requirement_evidence.commit_for_task_review directly (returned resolved:True, commit_sha=0526323, refusal:None - a review turn would be silently handed the pre-fix code with total, unearned confidence). Direction is not fixed either way: the operator's checkout could equally be AHEAD of the described work, giving a false-positive footprint instead. Three remedies are plausible and this run picked none: (1) record() validates the captured footprint against a locator that parses as a commit-ish and refuses or warns on mismatch; (2) for an operator actor, resolve the footprint from the locator's named commit/branch when one is given, falling back to workspace.root only when it is not; (3) surface the footprint (and any mismatch) in the record-evidence API response, which today never reports it at all (a second, smaller finding folded into F71's write-up: POST .../project/spec/evidence's handler calls _evidence_view(evidence) with no footprint= argument, unlike every sibling call site in the same file, so the response reads 'footprint: null' even when a footprint WAS captured). Left unfixed; task-7f49caae3c6d in proj-bad259c0c9f2 left under_review as inspectable evidence, reproduction script at scripts/drive/t_evidence_footprint.py.

NEEDS A DECISION: F70 (scripts/drive/FINDINGS.md, severity A) - found live iteration 10, driving Q6 against a fresh project. An operator (or any API caller) can PATCH a task straight from completed to under_review without reassigning it away from its own author. hub/hub/scheduler.py's WITH_REVIEWER_LOOP_TASK_STATUSES branch (~1214-1232) trusts under_review status alone to mean 'a reviewer already holds this' and never checks that the assignee differs from whoever completed it - so the task sits silently 'in flight' forever, and because _agents_that_are_free also counts that stuck assignee as busy, it becomes permanently unrecruitable as a reviewer for every OTHER task in the project too, with zero error and zero event naming the cause. NEW, measured 2026-08-27 (iteration 6): a test that mocks `PtySession.spawn` with a SHARED session object (`MagicMock(return_value=_completed_session(...))`) can hang the whole pytest process forever, not just fail, if a second real turn for the same agent reuses that same mock. `agent_trigger.py`'s own turn-completion path calls `schedule_agent` again UNCONDITIONALLY whenever a turn ends with entries still queued ('a turn ending with queued entries starts the next turn without waiting for operator input') - this is not something a test opts into, it fires for every job/flow-fired queue with more than one entry. If the second spawn reuses an already-exhausted `read.side_effect` list, the 3rd `pty.read()` call raises `StopIteration`, and `asyncio.Future.set_exception` explicitly refuses to accept `StopIteration` (a PEP-479-era guard) - so `run_in_executor`'s own exception-reporting callback raises, the future is never resolved, and `await` on it hangs with the event loop sitting idle (near-zero CPU, easy to mistake for 'still working'). Always give `spawn` a `side_effect` that produces a FRESH session object per call (e.g. a lambda) when a test's agent has more than one queued entry, even if the test only intends to observe the first turn - self-continuation may still spawn a second one inside the same `_drain()`. To localise a hang like this: `faulthandler`'s thread-dump only shows 'sitting in the event loop', not useful; instead schedule a diagnostic `asyncio.create_task` that sleeps a few seconds then calls `t.print_stack()` on every `asyncio.all_tasks()` - that shows the actual awaited coroutine chain.

Before `every-run-knows-its-task` group 2, only direct-`task_id` operator triggers ever set that field, so a job/flow-fired task sat at `assigned` for its ENTIRE run - several pre-existing tests asserted this as if it were permanent (`test_loop_fire_claims_the_oldest_pending_task` and 5 others found by running the FULL suite, not just touched files). method_reminders: THE OPERATOR'S ROUND DISCIPLINE, decided 2026-08-27 and binding on every change below. A change that does NOT yet have artifacts gets THREE separate rounds before any implementation: (R1) explore the codebase, then propose; (R2) review the proposal against the code and fix it; (R3) review again against the code and fix again. A change that ALREADY has artifacts gets ONE round: compare its artifacts to the codebase and make sure the spec is good. Each round is its own queue item and its own commit. Do NOT collapse rounds - the point is that the second and third readings happen with the first already written down, which is exactly what catches a proposal that reads plausibly and does not match the code. A round that finds nothing wrong must SAY SO explicitly and say what it checked; 'looks fine' with no enumeration means the round did not happen.
Use the real surface. Never simulate a step. If something has no API, that absence IS the finding - write it down and continue. This is how 'no integration step exists' surfaced.
Play the operator honestly, and leave something unanswered. A tester who answers everything never discovers which questions silently evaporate.

Watch the seams: between exploring and proposing, between an approved document and a task, between a completed task and a reviewed one, between one agent and the next. The defects are there, not inside a phase.
Read what the agent actually said. The transcript is evidence. Do not dismiss an agent's account of its own failure - verify it.
Follow peer-triggered work, not just what you triggered. Runs an agent starts by messaging another take a different path through the code, and that is where posture and continuity get lost.

Never accept 'the tests pass' as evidence. Run them yourself, then recompute a result by hand and compare. Check the rows, not the chat: an agent's summary of what it did is a claim, the rows are the fact.
A green suite agrees with broken behaviour more often than you expect. Mutation-check anything you claim: delete the line the test exists for, and watch a NAMED test fail.
The best evidence is the failure you did not stage. Watch for unprovoked failures and write them up when they happen.
Say when you contaminated your own test. Testing code you wrote yourself inherits your blind spots - a finding you did NOT make is weaker evidence, and the operator needs to know which is which.
Record what HELD, not only what broke. A gate that correctly refused something is a result the next session needs.
